summary.text: The giant tubeworm, Riftia pachyptila, is a polychaete worm that lives in large clusters around deep-sea hydrothermal vents in the East Pacific Rise and the Galapagos Rift.
Adults have no mouth or gut; a red plume takes in chemicals from the water, and bacteria living inside the worm provide its nutrition.
It can reach 3 m long and grows faster than any other known marine invertebrate, reaching 1.5 m in under two years.

items.prompt: A biologist cuts open an adult giant tubeworm hoping to see what it last ate. What will she find?

options.label: Half-digested shrimp in its gut
Bacteria-filled tissue but no gut
Vent minerals packed in its stomach
Filtered plankton in its intestine

items.explain: Adults have no mouth, digestive system or anus; instead a spongy tissue called the trophosome houses the bacteria that feed them.

items.prompt: Why is the feathery plume at the top of a giant tubeworm bright red?

options.label: It is dyed by the red food it eats
Red bacteria coat its outer surface
Its blood vessels are full of hemoglobin
Rust from vent iron stains the tissue

items.explain: The plume is packed with blood vessels, and its red colour comes from hemoglobin.

items.prompt: A young giant tubeworm settles at a brand-new vent. How long can it take to mature and grow to 1.5 m?

options.label: About fifty years
About ten years
A few centuries
Under two years

items.explain: It has the fastest growth rate of any known marine invertebrate, colonising a site, maturing and reaching 1.5 m in under two years.

items.prompt: A crab brushes against a giant tubeworm's plume. What does the worm do?

options.label: Pulls the plume in and plugs its tube
Stings the crab with its plume
Lets go and swims away from it
Squirts a cloud of sulfide at it

items.explain: When touched or threatened, it retracts the plume into its tube and seals the opening with the tip of a stiff support structure; the worms are sessile, so they cannot swim off.

items.prompt: Why do giant tubeworms crowd tightly around vents instead of spreading out across the seafloor?

options.label: Vents wash their waste away for them
Vents keep all predators far away
Vent water has much lower pressure
Vents supply chemicals their bacteria use

items.explain: Vents release chemicals such as hydrogen sulfide that the worm's bacteria use for chemosynthesis, and worms jostle for access to that vent fluid.

items.prompt: Hydrogen sulfide normally blocks the chemistry animals use to burn oxygen. How does Riftia keep carrying oxygen at sulfide-rich vents?

options.label: Its hemoglobin carries oxygen even with sulfide present
It stops breathing whenever sulfide levels rise
It only feeds in water that holds no sulfide
Its tube filters every trace of sulfide out

items.explain: Riftia's hemoglobins are unusual: they carry oxygen in the presence of sulfide without being inhibited, and they also bind sulfide for the bacteria.
